newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-ITF DISMISS AUSTRIAN DAVIS CUP PROTEST.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-ITF DISMISS AUSTRIAN DAVIS CUP PROTEST.

text.p: Austria have been ordered to forfeit $59,000 prize money for failing to complete their Davis Cup world group qualifier against Brazil in Sao Paulo last month.
Austria refused to complete the last three rubbers after world number three Thomas Muster walked off court in protest at what he felt was the threatening behaviour of the home crowd.
But Austrian attempts to have the tie replayed at a neutral venue ended in failure on Monday when the International Tennis Federation (ITF) rubber-stamped Brazil's 4-1 victory.
They also confirmed on-site fines totalling $8,000 on Muster, who appeared in person to argue his case.
The Austrian number one said conditions were the most hostile he had encountered in his career, but ITF president Brian Tobin said few of Muster's allegations had been substantiated.
"We felt the situation didn't justify the walkout," Tobin said. "Most of the things spectators were accused of were not substantiated."
Muster complained the Brazilian crowd insulted and spat at him and doubles partner Udo Plamberger and said they had thrown small stones on to the court.

The Austrian team promptly withdrew from the reverse singles and flew home early, forfeiting their remaining matches and handing Brazil a victory which put them back into the world group after a three-year absence.

The Austrian Tennis Federation backed Muster and prepared a 30-page report which was also critical of the court surface and the quality of television coverage. The federation claimed Muster had been severely provoked.

But Luis Noriega, a spokesman for the Brazilian organisers, said: "If anyone spat it was Muster. He spat blatantly on the court and made obscene gestures to the crowd. The crowd was noisy but that is the behaviour of a Latin crowd."
Muster spearheaded Austria's most successful Davis Cup campaign in 1990 when they reached the world group semifinals.
As he left the ITF offices to fly home, Muster denied he had exaggerated his complaints.
"He said he regretted his action," Tobin said. "I don't think a professional sportsmen should desert the ship."
